questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman was found to have a raised serum creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL. She had undergone a kidney transplantation 9 months earlier. She was asymptomatic. Her immunosuppressive medications included tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. She had normal renal function on previous follow-up visits and had a baseline creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL. No changes were made to her medications recently. Her urinalysis was normal.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: BK virus nephropathy BK virus nephropathy is asymptomatic and should be suspected when there is an unexplained rise in serum creatinine in kidney transplant recipients. The diagnosis is confirmed by the identification of decoy cells in urine cytology and detection of BK virus nucleic acid in urine and blood. Other options listed are typically symptomatic.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q40

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman presented with progressive headaches, confusion, and difficulty in walking. She was known to have relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis and had been treated with monthly natalizumab for 3 years. On examination she had bilateral lower extremity weakness. Sensation was intact. She had some word-finding difficulties. There was no photophobia or neck stiffness. Investigations: CT head: no mass effect seen. Asymmetric low attenuation foci in the periventricular and subcortical white matter.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Stop natalizumab and consider plasma exchange

questions.explanation: Stop natalizumab and consider plasma exchange Based on risk factors and clinical presentation, the diagnosis is most likely to be progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). The recommended treatment is to immediately stop the natalizumab, and some experts also recommend plasma exchange.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q37

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presented with fevers, dyspnea, cough, and an erythematous rash. He was day 115 after an HLAmismatched and T-cell-depleted allogeneic stem cell transplant for lymphoma. He had been treated at day 70 with prednisone for acute graft versus host disease. Investigations: Total white cell count 6.7 ×109/L CT chest: bilateral ground glass opacities BAL cultures and stains negative Urinalysis revealed hematuria with no bacteria on the stain Serum cytomegalovirus PCR undetectable
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Adenovirus The patient in this case is immunocompromised and at risk for many opportunistic infections, but the T-celldepleted graft and graft versus host disease are both risk factors for disseminated adenovirus infection. The hematuria in the case suggests adenovirus or BK virus, but BK virus would not cause the pneumonitis. HSV and VZV would be unusual causes of hematuria and diagnostic testing for CMV was negative.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q7

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of progressive right arm weakness and a 1-week history of increasing confusion and word-finding difficulties. He was known to have HIV , and although previously on ART he had been lost to clinical care and follow-up 3 years earlier. On physical exam, neurologic exam was notable for 3/5 strength in the right upper extremity and an expressive aphasia. Investigations: MRI of the brain: there are multiple discrete lesions in the cortical white matter and basal ganglia, which are hyperintense on the T2-weighted imaging sequences. CD4 count 125 cells/μL HIV viral load 45,200 copies/mL Serum RPR negative Serum cryptococcal antigen negative Toxoplasma IgG negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Antiretroviral therapy The most likely diagnosis given the clinical syndrome and characteristic findings on MRI of the brain is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by JC virus. The recommended treatment for PML is immediate initiation of ART to achieve immune reconstitution. Treatments such as cidofovir, cytarabine, and 5HT2a serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as mirtazapine have been tested but have shown no or inconclusive clinical benefit. The antivirals aciclovir and ganciclovir do not have activity against JC virus.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q22

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with polycystic kidney disease underwent cadaveric renal transplantation, cytomegalovirus D/R-, HLA-incompatible. His immunosuppressive regimen consisted of tacrolimus, prednisolone, and mycophenolate mofetil. He was taking trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole for PCP prophylaxis. At 10 months after the transplantation he reported rose-colored urine. He was otherwise well. Urinalysis: leukocytes ++, hematuria +++ Creatinine 238 μmol/L
questions.lead_in: What investigation is most likely to be diagnostic?
questions.explanation: Renal biopsy This is a case of BK virus nephropathy. The definitive diagnosis of BKVN requires a renal biopsy showing polyomavirus-induced cytopathic changes in tubular or glomerular epithelial cells.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q46

questions.question: A patient is put on TNF-a inhibitor for rheumatoid arthritis. She now presents with signs and symptoms of meningitis. CSF cultures are positive for E. coli and B. fragilis.

parts.text: Prior to starting the TNF-a inhibitor, what screening test could have been done to prevent this?
What bacterial etiology should be screened for before starting this treatment?
What are 2 viruses (non-herpesviridae) that can be re-activated on this treatment?

cohort_answer.text: Strongyloides serology. || TB. || Hep B, JC virus (Hep C can be exacerbated).

parts.text: Name three laboratory tests that can be used to evaluate for BK nephropathy.

questions.model_answer: Three tests for BK nephropathy: (1) Quantitative BK viral load (PCR) in plasma - high negative predictive value for excluding nephropathy (2) Urine cytology for 'decoy cells' (infected epithelial cells with viral inclusions) (3) Renal allograft biopsy with immunohistochemistry (SV40 T-antigen staining) - the diagnostic gold standard.

parts.text: Name three genitourinary diseases BK virus can cause.

questions.model_answer: Three genitourinary diseases caused by BK virus: (1) Hemorrhagic cystitis (2) BK virus-associated nephropathy/interstitial nephritis (in renal transplant recipients) (3) Ureteral stenosis.

parts.text: What are 4 neurological manifestations of JC virus?

cohort_answer.text: PML (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy); Cognitive/behavioural changes (36-54%); Motor/hemiparesis (33-45%); Gait incoordination/ataxia (35%); Visual changes (19-41%); Speech/language (24-40%)

questions.question: 50yo M HIV positive patient with CD4 count 50copies/mL, non-compliant with ART presenting with ataxia and vague neuro symptoms, no headaches. No focal neuro symptoms on exam. No history of travel, lives in Toronto. No LP given. MRI brain shows diffuse multifocal lesions.

parts.text: Give 4 pathogens and their associated syndromes to explain the clinical presentation.

questions.model_answer: Four pathogens and associated syndromes explaining diffuse multifocal brain lesions with ataxia in advanced untreated HIV (CD4 <50): (1) JC virus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), causing multifocal, non-enhancing white matter lesions with subacute focal deficits, ataxia, and cognitive decline. (2) Toxoplasma gondii - toxoplasmic encephalitis, typically multiple ring-enhancing lesions with mass effect, though can present with ataxia/ill-defined symptoms if cerebellar involvement. (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis, diffuse periventricular lesions, altered mental status, can cause ataxia and cranial nerve findings. (4) Primary CNS lymphoma (EBV-associated) - single or multiple enhancing mass lesions, can present with diffuse neurologic symptoms and ataxia depending on location.

questions.question: Causes of hemorrhagic cystitis 5 days post allo cell transplant

parts.text: Causes of hemorrhagic cystitis 5 days post allo cell transplant
4 causes if it happened 5 months post tx

questions.model_answer: a) Causes of hemorrhagic cystitis at 5 days post allo-HSCT (early, pre-engraftment): chemotherapy/conditioning toxicity - cyclophosphamide (acrolein metabolite) or busulfan-based conditioning regimen toxicity; radiation cystitis from total body irradiation. b) Four causes if occurring at 5 months post-transplant (late, viral): (1) BK virus (most common late cause). (2) Adenovirus. (3) CMV. (4) JC virus (less common) - also consider GVHD-related or drug-induced causes.
questions.beyond_mandell: Based on established HSCT complications literature

parts.text: Provide 2 complications of BK virus infection in an immunosuppressed host

cohort_answer.text: Virus | Disease association | Population. BK PyV | PVAN (polyomavirus associated nephropathy) | KT; | Hemorrhagic cystitis | BMT; | Rare | CNS and PNA, Ureteric Stenosis. JC PyV | PML | HIV/AIDS, MS and psoriasis; | PVAN | KT; | Rare | CNS and PNA. (Notes: KT = kidney transplant)

questions.question: AM 8. BK nephropathy - What are 3 modes of laboratory tests to do for diagnosis? (1.5)

parts.text: What are 3 modes of laboratory tests to do for diagnosis?

cohort_answer.text: DNA NAT (urine - highly sensitive, less specific, look for viral loads >2.5x10^7; serum - highly specific to trigger biopsy if >4 log or change in meds); Urine cytology (decoy cells, classic for polyomavirus); Histopathology (gold standard - renal biopsy with IF stain SV40). Algorithm: Urine NAT -> Serum NAT -> Histopathology (serology not useful for diagnosis).

questions.question: PM 5. List 3 urogenital diseases from BK virus infection (1.5)

parts.text: List 3 urogenital diseases from BK virus infection

cohort_answer.text: Urogenital: Hemorrhagic cystitis; Interstitial nephritis; Ureteric stenosis. (Extra-urogenital: Encephalitis; Pneumonia/Pneumonitis.)

questions.question: Gentleman with HIV has lived in Toronto his entire life. Noncompliant with ART and CD4 is 50. Presents with 3 weeks of altered LOC and ataxia. MRI shows scattered white matter lesions without mass effect.

parts.text: What are the 4 most likely organisms and diseases they cause?

cohort_answer.text: PML - JC Virus; CMV; HSV; VZV; TB (possible to get hydrocephalus though). Other differentials more likely to have mass effect/increased ICP: Toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcal. Non-infectious ddx: CNS lymphoma (causes mass effect).

questions.question: What are 3 ways to assess for BK virus in a renal transplant patient (specifically microbiological test)?

parts.text: 3 ways to assess for BK virus

cohort_answer.text: Quantitative PCR in plasma (100% sens, 88% spec); quantitative PCR in urine (100% sens, 78% spec); urine cytology - infected "decoy" cells with large nuclei and single large basophilic intranuclear inclusion (sens 25%, spec 84%); histopathology - kidney biopsy with Haufen (characteristic but not specific).

parts.text: What are 3 manifestations of BK virus?

cohort_answer.text: BKVAN (BK virus nephropathy) -> in renal transplant patients. Hemorrhagic cystitis -> HSCT patients. (BK virus latent infection -> asymptomatic). Ureteric stenosis

parts.text: Man from Toronto with HIV with CD4 50, 3 weeks worsening ataxia and difficulty concentrating and memory loss, probably other symptoms, no focal neuro though. MRI shows no space occupying lesions but does show multifocal white matter disease. What are four organisms implicated and the diseases they cause?

questions.model_answer: Four organisms and the diseases they cause in this HIV patient (CD4 50) with subacute encephalopathy and multifocal white matter disease without mass lesions: (1) JC virus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) (2) HIV itself - HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder/HIV encephalopathy (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis (4) Varicella-zoster virus - VZV vasculopathy/leukoencephalitis.

questions.question: 14 year old female who underwent allogeneic stem cell transplant 21 days ago for relapsed AML. She is experiencing dysuria and hematuria. You suspect BK virus hemorrhagic cystitis.

parts.text: What are 4 risk factors for BK virus hemorrhagic cystitis in allogeneic stem cell transplant?
What urine based test other than blood can be used for diagnosis?
What are 2 antivirals from different classes that can be used for treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Four risk factors for BK hemorrhagic cystitis after allogeneic HSCT: (1) myeloablative conditioning regimen (2) acute graft-versus-host disease (3) BKV seropositivity/high anti-BKV IgG before transplant (4) greater degree of immunosuppression/lymphopenia (also unrelated or HLA-mismatched donor).
b) Urine-based test: urine cytology for decoy cells, or quantitative BK viral PCR (viruria) - BK viral load in urine typically exceeds that in blood in cystitis.
c) Two antivirals from different classes: (1) Cidofovir (nucleotide analog DNA polymerase inhibitor) (2) A fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin (inhibits BKV-encoded DNA gyrase/topoisomerase); leflunomide (immunomodulatory DHODH inhibitor) is another accepted alternative-class option.

questions.question: Q72 2023 Day 1. AutoSCT with BK hemorrhagic cystitis. (VIRUSES)

parts.text: 4 risk factors
One urinary test to diagnose, in addition to her symptoms
Which 2 antiviral drugs to treat

cohort_answer.text:
4 risk factors: Myeloablative conditioning regimens (HLA mismatch higher risk); haploidentical donor; GVHD (acute and chronic); CMV reactivation; male sex.
Urinary test/symptoms: Typically BK viruria; BKPyV serum can help with diagnosis; BK viremia >10,000 copies/mL more likely to occur; symptoms - cystitis (dysuria, urgency, abdominal pain), hematuria, AKI.
2 antiviral drugs: Intravesicular and IV Cidofovir (no RCT data, some observational studies); Brincidofovir (pro-drug of Cidofovir); Leflunomide (has some antiviral properties against BKV).

questions.question: Polyomaviruses

parts.text: What are two viruses from the polyomavirus family and what is the MOST common clinic syndrome?
Fill in the blanks, polyomavirus is an ______ (RNA or DNA) virus and has ______ (an envelop or no envelope)
How do you manage polyomavirus infection in someone with HIV/AIDS.

questions.model_answer:
a) Two polyomaviruses and their most common clinical syndrome: JC virus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML); BK virus - hemorrhagic cystitis/BK nephropathy (chiefly in transplant recipients).
b) Polyomaviruses are DNA viruses with no envelope (non-enveloped).
c) Management of polyomavirus (JCV/PML) infection in HIV/AIDS: no specific effective antiviral exists - management is reduction/reversal of immunosuppression by initiating or optimizing combination antiretroviral therapy to achieve immune reconstitution, which is associated with improved survival.

questions.question: 24. What are 4 neurological manifestations of JC virus? (4)

parts.text: What are 4 neurological manifestations of JC virus? (4)

cohort_answer.text: PML (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy) - Classic (no edema around lesions on MRI) or IRIS (edema around lesions on MRI). JC virus granule cell neuronopathy - focus of infection in cerebellum with destruction of granule cells, diagnosed on cerebellar biopsy or PCR. JC virus meningitis. JC virus encephalitis/encephalopathy - gray matter infection.

questions.question: Clinical scenario suggestive of PML. "The diagnosis of PML should be suspected in patients who present with subacute neurologic deficits in the setting of immunosuppression or immunomodulatory therapy if brain MRI reveals focal or multifocal white matter lesions, generally without mass effect, that do not conform to vascular territories."

parts.text: How do you dx?

cohort_answer.text: MRI with and without GAD – lesions typically white matter sparing cortex but do not conform to vascular territory. CSF: mild pleocytosis, slightly elevated protein, normal glucose. PCR 72-92% sensitive, 92-100% specific. Brain Bx (Gold standard): demyelination, bizarre astrocytes, enlarged oligodendroglial nuclei

parts.text: Cause?

cohort_answer.text: PML caused by reactivation of the polyomavirus JC (JCV). Asymptomatic primary infection occurs in childhood, antibodies found in 86% of adults. JCV remains latent in kidneys and lymphoid organs, but in profound cellular immunosuppression can reactivate

parts.text: Treatment/Management/Workup

cohort_answer.text: Treatment: immune reconstitution – if HIV+, start ARV; if not HIV+, consider reducing immunosuppression. No antivirals. Workup: Clinical exam, MRI, CSF for JCV PCR, +/- brain bx

parts.text: What are 3-ways to assess for BK virus in a renal transplant patient (specifically microbiological test)

cohort_answer.text: BK virus blood qPCR - regular intervals following transplant; BKVL > 10,000 copies/mL -> moderate PPV for rejection from BKVAN. Urine microscopy to look for 'decoy cells'. Urine BK PCR. Urine Haufen - requires electron microscopy, not widely available
